rules.title: S.2983, An Act prohibiting algorithmic rent setting
rules.requirement: This is a pending Senate bill to prohibit algorithmic rent setting. The bill now sits in Senate Ways and Means. The captured pages do not include the bill text, so covered software, prohibited conduct, penalties and the effective date are unknown.

rules.title: Statewide prohibition on local rent control (G.L. c. 40P)
rules.requirement:
No city or town may enact, maintain or enforce rent control of any kind. The only exception is for a city or town that accepts chapter 40P, which may adopt rent control regulation subject to these limits:
- Owner compliance becomes entirely voluntary six months after initial adoption.
- The regulation may not cover occupancy, services, evictions, condominium conversion or removal of properties from regulation.
- It may not apply to units of owners holding fewer than ten rental units, or to units with a fair market rent above $400.
- The municipality must compensate owners from general funds for the difference between fair market rent and the controlled rent.

Rent control is defined to include any regulation that in any way requires below-market rents for residential properties.
rules.key_value: Statewide ban on local rent control. Narrow exception for accepting municipalities: voluntary after 6 months, not for owners of fewer than 10 units or units with fair market rent over $400, and owners compensated from municipal general funds.

coverage.landlord_size_condition: Any local regulation under the exception may not apply to units owned by a person or entity owning fewer than ten rental units.
coverage.summary: Bars rent control in every Massachusetts city and town, except a voluntary, compensated regulation in a municipality that accepts c. 40P. That regulation is limited to owners of ten or more units and to units with fair market rent of $400 or less.
coverage.owner_conditions: Exception regulation cannot reach owners of fewer than ten rental units.
coverage.other_conditions: Exception available only to a city or town that accepts c. 40P. Units with fair market rent above $400 are excluded. The regulation may not cover occupancy, services, evictions, condominium conversion or removal from regulation.

rules.exemptions: Exception to the ban: a city or town accepting c. 40P may adopt voluntary, compensated rent control regulation within the limits of § 4(a)-(c).
rules.effective_date_note: The official text gives no enactment or effective date. DX14 (secondary) says the original rent control ban was passed by voters in 1994; the official text does not confirm this.
rules.quoted_span: No city or town may enact, maintain or enforce rent control of any kind, except that any city or town that accepts this chapter may adopt rent control regulation that provides:
rules.review_note: This statute does not itself cap rents. It is kept as the state-versus-local precedence rule for rent increase limits. The documents do not say whether any municipality has accepted c. 40P. Initiative Petition 25-21, which would have repealed c. 40P, failed (barred from the 2026 ballot), so c. 40P remains in force. Boston's rent stabilization home-rule petition H.3744 also failed, so no MA municipal rent control is shown.
rules.source_notes: The SJC opinion in Cella v. Attorney General (DX03) quotes § 2 and § 3 of c. 40P and confirms the statewide prohibition.

also_supported_by.quoted_span: General Laws c. 40P, § 2, "broadly prohibits any regulatory scheme based upon or implementing rent control."

rules.title: Initiative Petition 25-21, An Initiative Petition to Protect Tenants by Limiting Rent Increases (barred from November 2026 ballot)
rules.requirement:
This proposed statewide initiative would have:
- struck G.L. c. 40P, the state ban on rent control;
- capped any annual rent increase for covered dwelling units at the lower of the annual Consumer Price Index increase or five percent.

On June 23, 2026, in Cella v. Attorney General, the SJC held the petition relates to religion under art. 48. The reason was its exemption for facilities operated solely for religious purposes. The court remanded for a judgment declaring the petition noncompliant and enjoining its placement on the November 2026 ballot.
rules.key_value: Proposed cap: lower of annual CPI increase or 5%. Never took effect.

new_construction_exemption.basis: newly constructed units less than 10 years old (per secondary source DX14)

unverifiable_exemptions: dwelling units in facilities operated solely for educational, religious, or nonprofit purposes
coverage.summary: Would have covered most residential rental units statewide ('covered dwelling units'). Exempt: owner-occupied buildings of four or fewer units, units under 10 years old, certain publicly regulated units, short-term rentals, and units in facilities operated solely for educational, religious or nonprofit purposes.
coverage.owner_conditions: Owner-occupied buildings with four or fewer units exempt (per DX14).
coverage.other_conditions: Short-term rentals and certain publicly regulated units exempt (per DX14).

rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied buildings with four or fewer units, newly constructed units less than 10 years old, certain publicly regulated units, short-term rentals, and units in facilities operated solely for educational, religious or nonprofit purposes. Only the last category is confirmed by the SJC opinion.
rules.effective_date_note: Never took effect. The SJC decision of June 23, 2026 bars placement on the November 2026 ballot. Proponents hinted at a new petition for the 2028 ballot.
citation_aliases: An Initiative Petition to Protect Tenants by Limiting Rent Increases
rules.quoted_span: the annual increase in Consumer Price Index or [five percent], whichever is lower
rules.review_note: The petition text is not captured. Its terms come from the SJC opinion's description, and the exemption list beyond the religious and educational facilities comes from a secondary blog (DX14). This is a failed measure and is kept separate from G.L. c. 40P, which remains in force.
rules.source_notes: DX14 (law blog) and DX15 (WBUR) describe the same SJC ruling. DX15 also mentions a compromise rent control bill that lawmakers did not pass before July 1; no details are given.

also_supported_by.quoted_span: Under the proposed law, annual rent increases would have been limited to the lesser of the annual increase in the Consumer Price Index or 5%.
The state’s Supreme Judicial Court ruled a ballot question seeking to bring rent control back to Massachusetts cannot go forward this November, because it includes a religious exemption.

rules.title: Source-of-income discrimination ban: public assistance and housing subsidy recipients (G.L. c. 151B, § 4(10))
rules.requirement:
Any person furnishing credit, services or rental accommodations may not discriminate against an individual for either of these reasons:
- the individual receives federal, state or local public assistance (including medical assistance) or housing subsidies (including rental assistance or rental supplements);
- any requirement of such a program.

Landlords therefore may not reject or treat applicants differently because of voucher, subsidy or assistance income. Section 4(7B) separately bars rental advertising that indicates a preference or limitation based on public assistance recipiency.
rules.key_value: Unlawful to discriminate against public assistance or housing subsidy recipients, or because of program requirements

coverage.summary: Applies to any person furnishing rental accommodations. Subsection 10 states no unit-count, construction-date or owner-occupancy exemption.
coverage.other_conditions: Protects recipients of public assistance and tenants receiving housing subsidies.

rules.effective_date_note: The document does not state when subsection 10 took effect.
rules.quoted_span: For any person furnishing credit, services or rental accommodations to discriminate against any individual who is a recipient of federal, state, or local public assistance, including medical assistance, or who is a tenant receiving federal, state, or local housing subsidies, including rental assistance or rental supplements, because the individual is such a recipient, or because of any requirement of such public assistance, rental assistance, or housing subsidy program.
rules.review_note: The owner-occupied two-family exemption in subsections 7 and 11 does not appear in subsection 10. The general protected-class housing provisions (subsections 6, 7, 11) are not extracted as separate screening records. Boston and Cambridge have complementary local source-of-income protections. State criminal-history screening rules (803 CMR 5) are not captured; see known_gaps.
rules.source_notes: Official statute text; no penalty or enforcement detail in this section.

rules.title: Fourteen-day notice to quit for nonpayment under a written lease (G.L. c. 186, § 11)
rules.requirement: When rent due under a written lease is unpaid, the landlord may end the lease with 14 days' written notice to quit. The tenant defeats termination by paying or tendering all rent due, with interest and costs of suit, on or before the answer day in the possession action. If nonpayment was caused by a government delay or failure in mailing or delivering a subsistence or rental payment, the court must continue the hearing at least 7 days to notify the agency. If all rent, interest and costs are tendered within that time, the court treats the tenancy as not terminated.
rules.key_value: 14 days' written notice to quit; cure by answer day; at least 7-day continuance for government payment delay

coverage.summary: Tenancies under a written lease where rent is unpaid; no unit-count, age or owner limits stated.

rules.effective_date_note: The text gives no effective date; current codified statute.
rules.quoted_span: Upon the neglect or refusal to pay the rent due under a written lease, fourteen days' notice to quit, given in writing by the landlord to the tenant, shall be sufficient to determine the lease, unless the tenant, on or before the day the answer is due, in an action by the landlord to recover possession of the premises, pays or tenders to the landlord or to his attorney all rent then due, with interest and costs of suit.
rules.review_note: This is a termination-notice rule, not a list of just causes. Massachusetts has no statewide just-cause requirement in the documents.

rules.title: Notice to terminate a tenancy at will (G.L. c. 186, § 12)
rules.requirement:
Either party may end a tenancy at will with three months' written notice. If rent is payable at intervals shorter than three months, notice equal to the rental interval or 30 days, whichever is longer, is enough.

Nonpayment rules:
- The landlord may terminate with 14 days' written notice to quit.
- A tenant who has not received a similar notice in the prior 12 months may prevent termination by paying the full rent due within 10 days of receipt.
- Every nonpayment notice must contain the statutory right-to-cure notification. If it is omitted, the cure period extends to the answer day, but the notice is otherwise valid.
- If nonpayment was caused by a government payment delay, the court must continue the hearing at least 7 days.
rules.key_value: 3 months' notice (or rental interval / 30 days if longer); 14-day nonpayment notice; 10-day cure once per 12 months

coverage.summary: Tenancies at will; no unit-count, building-age or owner-occupancy limits stated.

rules.effective_date_note: The text gives no effective date; current codified statute.
rules.quoted_span: In case of neglect or refusal to pay the rent due from a tenant at will, fourteen days' notice to quit, given in writing by the landlord to the tenant, shall be sufficient to determine the tenancy;
rules.review_note: Termination-notice rule. It does not limit grounds for ending a tenancy at will (no just-cause list).

rules.title: Massachusetts security deposit law (G.L. c. 186, § 15B)
rules.requirement:
A security deposit may not exceed the first month's rent. Holding and paperwork:
- Hold it in a separate interest-bearing Massachusetts bank account.
- Give a bank receipt within 30 days.
- Give a signed deposit receipt, and a statement of condition within 10 days of tenancy start or receipt, whichever is later.
- Keep deposit records for 2 years.

Interest and return:
- Pay 5% annual interest, or the lesser rate the bank paid.
- Return the deposit or balance within 30 days after the tenancy ends.
- Deductions are limited to unpaid rent or water charges, unpaid tax escalations, and reasonable damage beyond wear and tear, with a sworn itemized list.

Other rules:
- A successor in interest takes over the deposit and must notify the tenant within 45 days.
- Noncompliance forfeits the right to retain the deposit; certain violations carry treble damages plus 5% interest, costs and attorney's fees.
- Lease waivers are void.
- As amended effective August 1, 2025, regulations may allow an optional fee in lieu of a deposit; fee plus any deposit may not exceed 1 month's rent.
rules.key_value: Max deposit = first month's rent; return within 30 days; 5% interest (or lesser bank rate); treble damages

rules.title: Broker fees: licensing and payment only by the party who engaged the broker (G.L. c. 112, § 87DDD½)
rules.requirement:
Only a licensed broker or salesperson may engage in the business of finding dwelling accommodations for prospective tenants for a fee. As amended effective August 1, 2025:
- A licensed broker or salesperson may contract solely with the prospective tenant or solely with the landlord or landlord's agent.
- Any fee must be paid only by the party (lessor or tenant) who originally engaged and contracted with the broker or salesperson.
rules.key_value: Broker fee paid only by the party that engaged the broker; broker represents one side only; licensing required

coverage.summary: Rental residential property where a broker or salesperson is engaged for a fee to find a tenant or a dwelling.
coverage.other_conditions: Applies where a licensed broker or salesperson is engaged for a fee.

rules.effective_date_note: The amended text is effective August 1, 2025 under St. 2025, c. 9, § 43 (see § 136). The licensing sentence predates the amendment.
rules.quoted_span: Any fee shall only be paid by the party, lessor or tenant who originally engaged and entered into a contract with the licensed broker or salesperson.
rules.review_note: Broker disclosure rules in 254 CMR 7 are not captured; see known_gaps.
rules.source_notes: Official legislature page showing both the pre- and post-August 1, 2025 text.
